intro: A melody for violas and cellos alternates with a C-major fanfare, then changes through progressively smaller note values and a minor-mode detour. The movement ends in A♭ major: its C-major proclamations are interruptions, not its destination.
question: How can a variation change the surface while preserving the shape of a phrase?

cues.title: Violas and cellos sing
cues.text: The opening melody belongs to violas and cellos in octaves, above plucked double basses. Its dotted figures fit a three-quaver bar. The violins do not begin as the principal melodic voice.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf full score, printed p. 22, first system; also Mutopia 1437, viola.ly, violoncello.ly and basso.ly. This describes the opening scoring, not an isolated machine-identified entrance. The report begins at low relative level, around −24 dB.

cues.title: Unequal notes, connected phrases
cues.text: Keep the opening’s long-short dotted figures in mind as the phrase passes between orchestral groups. Later variations will fill the same melodic outline with more notes, so its direction and cadences are useful landmarks.
cues.evidence: The score’s opening dotted melody is ornamented in subsequent variations. This is a comparison across the movement, not a claim that a particular instrument enters at 0:36.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: A fanfare in C
cues.text: In this contrasting passage, C major replaces the opening’s A♭ major and trumpets and timpani reinforce the orchestral statement. The change is not simply a louder version of the opening: the tonal centre and instrumental weight change together.
cues.evidence: The score supplies C major and the trumpet–timpani scoring. The report has a boundary at 1:16 and a large relative-level rise from 1:10 to 1:25, with C–E–G prominent. These locate the passage, not an exact first chord.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The first varied cycle
cues.text: As the fanfare’s aftermath clears, the A♭-major melody returns with a more continuous stream of notes. Listen for the original phrase beneath the decoration; a busier surface need not mean a faster underlying beat.
cues.evidence: The score restores the lower-string melody in semiquavers. The 1:50 boundary and quiet 1:50–2:05 span locate the approach to the estimated 1:56 return. No bar alignment or beat measurement is claimed.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Two aristocratic dedicatees
cues.text: The Fifth is dedicated to Prince Lobkowitz and Count Razumovsky. The Sixth Symphony bears the same two names. Patronage links the companion works, although their musical designs differ.
cues.evidence: Eastman School of Music, general information and dedication: https://www.esm.rochester.edu/beethoven/symphony-no-5/

cues.title: The contrast happens again
cues.text: The varied cycle again approaches the C-major fanfare. Compare the contrast with its first appearance: the decorated A♭-major melody can change while the broader alternation between lyrical writing and proclamation remains recognisable.
cues.evidence: The score repeats the C-major trumpet statement after the first variation. Relative level rises from −19.4 dB at 3:10 to −10.1 at 3:15, then reaches −5.6 at 3:30; a boundary occurs at 3:16.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A bass that slips downward
cues.text: In the links after the fanfares, follow the bass rather than looking for a new tune. Beethoven writes a chromatic descent through E, E♭, D and D♭ towards C before redirecting the music towards A♭.
cues.evidence: Mutopia 1437, violoncello.ly, explicitly writes the chromatic bass after both early fanfares. The report’s quiet 3:35–3:55 passage is consistent with the second link, but the individual bass notes are not timed.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Four years of work
cues.text: Beethoven began sketching the Fifth in 1804 and completed it in 1808. Work on Fidelio, the Op. 59 quartets and the Appassionata intervened. The symphony grew alongside chamber music, opera and piano writing.
cues.evidence: Eastman School of Music, composition history: https://www.esm.rochester.edu/beethoven/symphony-no-5/

cues.title: Space after the elaboration
cues.text: Around this quieter passage, the densely decorated string writing gives way to a wind-led continuation. Listen for the distinction between a melody that moves in small notes and an accompaniment that leaves gaps around each attack.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf score, printed pp. 29–30: fermata, detached string accompaniment and successive clarinet, bassoon and flute writing. The report has a strong boundary at 5:04, its quietest windows at 5:05–5:10, and reduced brightness. The scoring is read from the score, not separated from the audio.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Another C-major arrival approaches
cues.text: The wind-led continuation prepares another broad fanfare. Keep the earlier C-major statements in mind: their recurrence helps organise a stretch whose smaller phrases have become increasingly elaborate.
cues.evidence: The score’s third C-major statement follows the woodwind elaboration. The report rises from −25.8 dB at 5:50 through −17.2 at 5:55 to −6.6 at 6:00; the 6:00 boundary anchors the approaching arrival, not this cue’s display time.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The fanfare withdraws
cues.text: After the broad statement, the orchestra withdraws into a much quieter stretch. Listen for short figures and changing harmonic colour rather than expecting the C-major proclamation to continue at the same weight.
cues.evidence: Relative level falls from −4.6 dB at 6:10 to −27.5 at 6:25, and stays near −28 through 6:40. The strongest boundary is at 6:24. This evidence establishes the withdrawal, not the exact onset of the score’s later A♭-minor writing.

cues.title: Major and minor versions
cues.text: Within this later episode, compare the altered, minor-coloured figures with the opening melody. The eventual full A♭-major return restores more than volume: it recovers the opening’s tonal identity after a stretch of altered pitches.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf score, printed pp. 32–33, gives the minor-coloured transformation and subsequent full-ensemble return. The report’s 7:10 boundary precedes a large rise around 7:20–7:30; the harmonic account comes from the score, not the unstable machine key labels.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A shared premiere concert
cues.text: On 22 December 1808 the Fifth and Sixth symphonies were first performed at Vienna’s Theater an der Wien. Beethoven’s programme also included the Fourth Piano Concerto and Choral Fantasy. The two symphonies reached the public in the same evening.

cues.title: A more mobile ending
cues.text: The coda includes a passage marked “Più moto” — more movement — before “Tempo I” restores the original pace. Follow the small accompaniment figures as well as the melody: Beethoven changes the gait without abandoning A♭ as the home key.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf score, printed pp. 34–35, contains Più moto and Tempo I. The report’s quiet 8:15–8:25 windows have 3.0–3.4 onsets per second before a boundary at 8:32 and a level rise. These support a broad coda placement, not the exact tempo-change bars.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Quiet does not mean finished
cues.text: The closing span makes room for quiet sustained harmony before another increase in activity. Listen through the drop in level: a phrase can sound settled while the movement still has a further cadence to make.
cues.evidence: Relative level falls from −16.8 dB at 9:00 to −27.4 at 9:05; a boundary appears at 9:12. Level and onset activity increase again around 9:35–9:40. No particular held chord is identified from the report.

cues.title: A♭ is the destination
cues.text: The last cadences confirm A♭ major, the key of the opening melody. C major has supplied conspicuous contrasts, but it does not take over this movement’s ending. Listen for the difference between a recurring interruption and the final home key.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf score, printed p. 36, ends on A♭ after E♭-to-A♭ cadential figures. The report’s final minute has persistent A♭–C–E♭ content; the score establishes the cadence, not the report’s differing local key estimates.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: A chromatic bass leads back to A♭
transitions.how: The C-major fanfare leaves its E natural exposed in a quiet link. The bass descends by semitone through E♭, D and D♭ towards C, then turns through D♭ to E♭, the dominant of A♭. Violas and cellos recover the opening melody with semiquavers filling its dotted outline. Brass weight falls away; the returning contour, bass route and lighter texture make the connection audible without a new tempo heading.
transitions.evidence: Mutopia 1437, violoncello.ly, gives the chromatic bass and decorated return; Breitkopf printed pp. 23–24. The estimated join at 1:56 follows the 1:50 boundary and quiet 1:50–2:05 windows. No individual bass note or first variation attack is aligned.

transitions.title: The same route gains smaller notes
transitions.how: The second C-major statement again withdraws through the chromatic bass link. This time the lower-string melody returns in demisemiquavers, with faster internal motion around its familiar pitches. The progression leads back to A♭ as before; the changed subdivision, rather than a new theme or metre, starts the next cycle. Later in this span Beethoven moves the elaboration into the winds before another C-major fanfare.
transitions.evidence: Mutopia 1437, violoncello.ly, distinguishes the semiquaver and demisemiquaver returns; Breitkopf printed pp. 27–30. Boundaries at 3:50 and 3:54 and the changing onset activity around 3:55–4:05 support a passage-level join at 3:56.

transitions.title: The proclamation gives way to fragments
transitions.how: The C-major fanfare diminishes instead of supplying a decisive ending. Trumpets and timpani withdraw while detached strings and woodwind figures continue the argument. The ensuing episode alters the familiar material through minor colouring, including A♭ minor, before rebuilding the opening theme. The join is a reduction of weight and continuity of small figures, not an instantaneous modulation to a wholly new tune.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf printed pp. 31–33 gives the diminuendo, reduced scoring and subsequent minor-mode writing. The report’s strongest boundary is 6:24, with relative level near −28 dB at 6:25–6:40. The exact A♭-minor onset is deliberately not equated with that audio boundary.

transitions.title: The opening melody regains orchestral weight
transitions.how: Small figures pass between winds and strings, and the rising activity builds into the opening melody in A♭ major. Winds and violins now reinforce a line first heard in violas and cellos, while lower strings supply rapid repeated notes. The material returns in a different distribution: melodic recognition and enlarged accompaniment coincide, rather than the orchestra merely repeating the opening at a higher level.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf printed p. 33 shows the growing string figures and tutti return. Relative level rises from −20.6 dB at 7:20 to −10.2 at 7:25 and −7.5 at 7:30. The estimated 7:24 join is passage-level, not a bar-aligned downbeat.

transitions.title: A smaller accompaniment changes the gait
transitions.how: The expanded return relinquishes its orchestral weight to a more compact closing span. In the Più moto passage, the bassoon carries the line over detached string figures; the changed pace comes within the same three-quaver metre. Tempo I subsequently restores the opening rate for the final expansion. A♭ remains the point of return, and the coda reuses the theme’s gestures instead of introducing a third main idea.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf printed pp. 34–36 supplies Più moto, the bassoon-led passage and Tempo I. The report is quieter at 8:10–8:25 with increased attack density from 8:15; 8:32 is a later boundary. The coda start at 8:12 is a broad formal estimate, not the precise Più moto marking.

timeline.note: Violas and cellos share the dotted melody above pizzicato double basses.
Wind replies and string continuation expand the opening phrase; brass fanfare instruments still wait.
The C-major statement adds trumpet and timpani weight to the full ensemble.
The fanfare withdraws into a quiet link with descending bass.
Lower strings begin the first decorated version of the opening melody.
Wind replies share the varied cycle with the strings.
The second fanfare restores the full C-major ensemble.
The chromatic link returns, with the fanfare’s brass weight removed.
Demisemiquavers further decorate the lower-string melody before the violin continuation.
Rapid lower-string figures expand against stronger orchestral punctuation.
After the fermata, successive wind phrases replace the continuous lower-string elaboration.
Another broad C-major fanfare gathers the whole orchestra.
Detached strings and wind figures carry the quieter, minor-coloured episode.
The opening melody is enlarged above rapid lower-string accompaniment.
The Più moto coda uses a bassoon line against detached strings; timing is approximate.
Tempo I restores wind replies and the opening phrase’s broader pace.
The closing crescendo and final cadences gather the orchestra around A♭.

facts: Christian Gottlob Neefe in Bonn; Haydn, Johann Georg Albrechtsberger and Antonio Salieri in Vienna
Bonn until 1792 · Vienna and its surrounding villages thereafter
Nine symphonies · five numbered piano concertos · 32 numbered piano sonatas · 16 string quartets · one opera
Progressive hearing loss documented in letters from 1801; conversation books used from 1818
composer.background:
Beethoven was born in Bonn in 1770, probably on 16 December, and baptised on 17 December. His father Johann sang in the electoral court chapel, and his grandfather Ludwig had been its Kapellmeister. The family name came from the Low Countries; the ‘van’ did not indicate nobility. Johann attempted to present his son as a child prodigy, but Beethoven’s more substantial training came from Christian Gottlob Neefe, who introduced him to Bach’s keyboard music and helped him obtain work as an organist. Playing viola in the court orchestra also gave him practical knowledge of instrumental and operatic repertory.

The Bonn years supplied more than a musical apprenticeship. The court of Elector Maximilian Franz, educated patrons and friends such as the Breuning family brought Beethoven into contact with Enlightenment literature and social ideas. After his mother’s death in 1787 and his father’s worsening incapacity, he assumed increasing responsibility for the household. In 1792 he left for Vienna to study with Haydn. The intended period of further training became permanent residence: the French occupation of Bonn in 1794 ended the old electoral establishment to which he might have returned.
composer.epithet: A pianist who turned small rhythmic cells into long arguments, then rebuilt the forms that contained them.
